                                         1   I.     INTRODUCTION

                                         2          Plaintiff Valerie Harvey noticed that her patio “was looking bare” and decided to find

                                         3   some patio furniture.1 She spent a half hour or so searching the websites of several other retailers

                                         4   before landing on World Market’s homepage at www.worldmarket.com,2 where she browsed for

                                         5   about twenty minutes before settling on a set of Jarle Molded Resin Outdoor Chairs (“Jarle

                                         6   Chairs”) and placed them in her Cart. When she opened her Cart she saw that for large, bulky

                                         7   items like furniture, World Market would charge her a flat $49.95 for shipping and handling and a

                                         8   $50 oversized item surcharge to cover the costs of delivery. She paused for about six minutes

                                         9   “contemplating” whether to incur the charges, but “decided to go ahead with the purchase” and

                                        10   “understood at that point that, if [she] went ahead with the purchase, [she] would pay the
                                             oversized item surcharge and the shipping charges.”3 She completed the transaction, the chairs

 SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA 94111-4070
   BRYAN CAVE LEIGHTON PAISNER LLP




                                        12   were delivered, and she was happy with her purchase.

                                        13          So why are we here? Harvey contends that by disclosing the shipping and handling and

                                        14   oversized item charges when she opened her Cart, rather than rolling them into the cost of the

                                        15   items, World Market ran afoul of Civil Code § 1770(a)(29)(A), a provision recently added to the

                                        16   Consumer Legal Remedies Act (“CLRA”), which prohibits “[a]dvertising, displaying, or offering

                                        17   a price for a good or service that does not include all mandatory fees or charges,” with exceptions.

                                        18   She also asserts claims under the Unfair Competition Law (Bus & Prof. Code s 17200 et seq.) and

                                        19   False Advertising Law (Bus & Prof. Code s 17500 et seq.) on the same theory.

                                        23   charges were clearly and conspicuously disclosed when she placed the items in her Cart and each

                                        24   step of the checkout process thereafter. The Court denied the motion, holding that “reliance is
